narrative:
Across Latin America the fielded unmanned inventory splits into three broad tiers. At the top sit a small number of MALE platforms, most of them imported or built under technology transfer: Brazil's Air Force has operated Elbit's Hermes 900 (locally RQ-900) since 2014 via AEL Sistemas, added units in 2021-22 and bought a replacement in 2024 after an operational loss, while Avionics Services builds the Caçador on IAI's Heron-1 under a 2013 cooperation agreement, with the earlier Embraer/AEL Harpia venture having placed the Hermes 450 in naval service until 2016. The only genuinely indigenous entries at this tier are Stella Tecnologia's Atobá (11 m span, 500 kg MTOW, 28 hours, 250 km datalink, maiden flight 2020) and its projected armed derivative Condor/Atobá XR (17 m span, 350 kg payload, 40 hours), alongside Argentina's still-unbuilt Vigía 2B and Hydra's aspirational S55 Ares.

The tactical middle tier is where domestic industry is real but shallow. Xmobots' Nauru 1000C (7.7 m span, 181 kg MTOW, 10 hours, 42 kg payload) was under Brazilian Army operational evaluation from 2022 to 2024; Stella's ship-capable Albatroz is in Navy testing; Colombia's CIAC fields the ART Quimbaya (5.24 m span, 74 kg MTOW, 8-10 hours, 100 km range), built on a technology transfer from Spain's Aertec TARSIS-75 and co-financed by Ecopetrol to protect pipelines from ELN attack. Hydra Technologies markets a four-platform family from the 4.06 m G3 Guerrero up to the 7.68 m S50 Kukulkan, though MTOWs, engines and avionics are undisclosed and vendor weaponization claims remain unverified. Below that sit small tactical and hand-launched systems: Carcará, FT-100 Horus, Coelum, Lipán M3, and CIAC's DRAGOM multirotor with its stated latent mortar/grenade attack profile.

Ground and naval systems barely exist: Brazil's Robô Expedicionário UGV and the EMGEPRON/TideWise Suppressor USV (launch 2026, commissioning 2027) lead, Argentina's PIÉLAGOS and VAE/VAD remain R&D, and no Mexican or Colombian programmes are documented.

Venezuela is the outlier, moving from near-zero capability to an armed arsenal - ANSU-100, Mohajer-6 with Qaem munitions, Orlan-10, and the Shahed-136-derived Zamora V-1 loitering munition - through Iranian and Russian assistance rather than domestic industry. Against all of this, VNSAs fly modified COTS DJI airframes, bomb-droppers and FPV kamikaze drones, and counter-UAS remains overwhelmingly imported and event-driven, with Brazil's DRONEBlocker and SCE-0100 the only credible domestic entries.

narrative:
Violent non-state actors have moved into the aerial domain that states once monopolized, and Latin America is among the sharpest expressions of that shift. More than 65 VNSAs worldwide now operate drones, and in a region where criminal networks, insurgencies and fragile governance converge, cheap commercial platforms, dual-use components and open-source know-how have let weaker actors offset conventional disadvantages. Contested Skies II frames the adoption curve as an asymmetric innovation cycle: unconstrained by procurement rules, bureaucratic inertia or legal limits, guerrillas and cartels test, learn and operationalize new tactics like startups, moving from surveillance and contraband logistics to psychological operations and kinetic strikes. Their penetration of the air domain is treated not merely as a tactical nuisance but as a direct Weberian challenge to territorial sovereignty and the state's monopoly on lethal force, compounding existing deficits of territorial control in Colombia and Mexico.

The tactical lineage runs from Syria to Mexico to Ukraine and back to the Andes. ISIS flew DJI drones for surveillance and propaganda from 2014 and fielded armed drones by 2017; Hizballah flew Iranian-made UAS into Israeli airspace as early as 2006 and conducted the first verified lethal non-state drone strike in September 2014. Ukraine then scaled FPV drones into mass battlefield use and became, in the framing of Contested Skies II, a platform for the global dissemination of FPV tactics, with Ukrainian intelligence suspecting Spanish-speaking volunteers entered the International Legion to learn FPV flying, some reportedly tied to cartels. Mexican cartels had already used commercial UAS for reconnaissance, smuggling and attacks before the war, adding FPVs, improvised explosive payloads and even their own counter-UAS systems in a criminal arms race.

Colombia is the central case of Contested Skies II. ELN and FARC dissidents have become 'techno guerrillas,' folding drones into the five classical pillars of guerrilla warfare — intelligence, security, mobility, surprise and sustainment — and shifting to a more offensive posture against civilians, soldiers, vehicles and bases. Attacks serve intelligence, signaling and learning functions as much as destruction, probing response times while generating propaganda and fear. Tactics evolve continuously: new flight profiles, longer endurance, night operations and deliberate jammer avoidance, mostly on modifiable commercial DJI airframes.

The state response lags. Colombia's unreleased field manuals teach spotting, dispersal and concealment via the DRON acronym but omit man-portable C-UAS employment, training curricula and sustainment, and focus narrowly on bomb-dropping quadcopters rather than FPV kamikazes, swarms or AI-enabled autonomy. Regional counter-drone posture remains event-driven, import-dependent and fragmented.

narrative:
Latin America's indigenous unmanned-systems industry is real but shallow. Production is concentrated in small- and medium-sized firms rather than large defence conglomerates, most domestically produced platforms are optimised for surveillance, agricultural or commercial use rather than military-grade applications, and governments do not consistently fund the R&D or place the procurement orders needed to scale prototypes into series production. The result is an industrial map full of demonstrators, short runs and pilot programmes: Argentina's most advanced airframes remain experimental, Colombia's flagship Quimbaya reads more as a pilot production programme than a fielded fleet, and even Brazil's Nauru 1000C spent 2022-24 in army operational evaluation rather than full procurement.

Component dependence is the central structural fact. Most regional drone programmes rely heavily on imported avionics — navigation, communications, flight control and mission control — plus foreign sensors and propulsion. Even Brazil's comparatively sovereign sector remains exposed to U.S. and Israeli inputs; Hydra Technologies withholds exact MTOWs, engines, avionics packages and datalink hardware, which suggests externally sourced engines, radios and high-end avionics; Colombia's Quimbaya rests on a technology transfer from Spain's Aertec (TARSIS-75), and the Caçador is a Heron-1 derivative built under a 2013 IAI agreement. This component dependency leaves the whole regional base vulnerable to supply-chain shocks, export restrictions and geopolitical pressure.

Four national models diverge sharply. Brazil runs a hybrid ecosystem — private OEMs (Xmobots, Stella, NEST, SantosLab, FT Sistemas) alongside service-led programmes, state development-bank and MoD support, a national UTM system (BR-UTM), and the region's only credible domestic counter-UAS base. Mexico is state-directed hybrid: one dominant private OEM (Hydra) plus SEMAR and SEDENA institutional R&D, given fresh political backing in September 2025. Argentina is institution-driven and budget-starved, with INVAP, FAdeA, CITEDEF and the Air Force's DGID sustaining a science base whose outputs rarely leave prototype stage. Colombia is overwhelmingly state-owned and operationally driven, with CIAC building purpose-fit platforms for asymmetric jungle and border warfare. Venezuela is the outlier — near-zero capability until the early 2000s, then a rapid build-out of armed and loitering systems enabled by Iranian and, secondarily, Russian support rather than domestic innovation.

Counter-UAS is the region's common failure. Only Brazil fields indigenous systems (IACIT's DRONEBlocker, the Army's SCE-0100). Argentina, Mexico and Colombia all rely on imports and ad hoc classified acquisitions, leaving a persistent gap in layered counter-drone capacity, doctrine and procurement agility.

narrative:
Latin America's unmanned-systems landscape is shaped less by what the region builds than by who supplies it from outside. Along the official procurement channel, Israel is the dominant high-end vendor: Elbit Systems supplies the Hermes 900 to the Brazilian Air Force as the RQ-900 through its local subsidiary AEL Sistemas, the Embraer-AEL Harpia joint venture put the Hermes 450 into Brazilian Navy service, and Israel Aerospace Industries' Heron-1 became the Caçador through a 2013 technical-cooperation agreement with Avionics Services. Spain contributes through technology transfer rather than sale: Colombia's flagship ART Quimbaya is derived from Aertec's TARSIS-75. The United States functions less as a supplier than as a gatekeeper, having led export restraint under the Missile Technology Control Regime, though its own footprint in the region includes the Dronebuster counter-drone system fielded by Colombian forces. Contested Skies I notes that even Brazil's comparatively sovereign sector remains exposed to U.S. and Israeli inputs.

The second pathway runs outside official regional channels entirely. Venezuela moved from effectively no unmanned capability in the early 2000s to one of the region's most diverse armed arsenals by 2025, an outcome attributed to more than two decades of cooperation with Iran and, to a lesser degree, Russia. Iranian involvement spans finished platforms (the Mohajer-6, supplied since 2020), locally assembled derivatives (the ANSU-100, linked to the Mohajer-2 and described as the region's first weaponized drone), design lineage for the Zamora V-1 loitering munition modelled on the Shahed-136, and the Qaem precision-guided munition line that Contested Skies I identifies as the critical escalation in lethality. Russia supplied the Orlan-10 tactical reconnaissance platform, reportedly in service since 2020, and Russian-made guided munitions arm the Antonio José de Sucre-100; a September 2025 bilateral pact formalised security, defence and technological cooperation.

China occupies a third position, supplying the region overwhelmingly through commercial retail rather than state transfer. DJI controls roughly 70 percent of global drone sales, and Beijing's 2023 export controls were aimed primarily at North American and European markets, leaving Latin America awash in Chinese commercial drones entering largely unimpeded. Those platforms — chiefly the Mavic line — are the systems most repurposed by cartels in Mexico and armed groups in Colombia. With Turkey interpreting MTCR restrictions loosely and Washington reclassifying MALE systems as aircraft, the barriers to further extra-regional supply are weakening on every front.

narrative:
The architecture restraining drone proliferation is eroding at both ends of the market. The Missile Technology Control Regime once anchored a presumption of export denial, and U.S. adherence meant sophisticated large systems reached only a handful of countries. Restraint is unwinding from two directions. Other suppliers interpret the regime loosely: Turkey exports Bayraktar systems across the Middle East, Africa and Eastern Europe despite MTCR membership, and Israel supplies Heron and Hermes MALE platforms plus Harop loitering munitions. Meanwhile the Trump administration reclassified large platforms such as the MQ-9 Reaper as 'aircraft' rather than 'missile systems' to ease exports and improve competitiveness against less selective proliferators. The chapter judges this will accelerate dissemination and may fuel an escalatory cycle in which cheaper access lowers the perceived cost of conflict.

China is the central enabler of dual-use proliferation. It has exported Wing Loong Class I combat systems to at least 17 countries while DJI controls roughly 70 percent of the global commercial market. Beijing's 2023 export controls on drones, engines, communication gear and anti-drone systems were framed as responsible-power restraint but functioned mainly as reciprocity against U.S. restrictions and as a response to European concerns about Chinese components in the Russia-Ukraine war. Because they targeted North American and European markets, Latin America remains awash in Chinese commercial drones entering largely unimpeded, even as China supplies around 80 percent of the critical electronics in Russian drones.

At the low end, small-drone diffusion is effectively ungoverned. National rules form a fragmented patchwork, no coherent international regime governs battlefield drone use, and the Hague and Geneva Conventions predate robotics and remote warfare. Norm evolution theory suggests great powers will not constrain technologies that serve their interests. Criminal procurement networks are also poorly understood: it is unclear how far they rely on e-commerce, gray-market intermediaries, or smuggling and diversion, and that gap blocks targeted controls.

The recommended response is layered. Interviewees urged governments to work with manufacturers so hard-wired geofencing, altitude caps and firmware restrictions stay intact. Globally, the chapter points to the U.S.-EU Trade and Technology Council, NATO, DIANA, the G7, G20 and WTO, and to extending MTCR logic and the 2016 Joint Declaration to subsystems and components. Regionally, it looks to the OAS Permanent Council, the Rio Treaty and the Inter-American Defense Board, with Mexico and Colombia coordinating given their operational experience. Absent this, fragile states risk becoming laboratories of tactical innovation.

narrative:
Investment in Latin American unmanned systems is governed by a single tension: fiscal constraint against the desire for sovereign capacity. Three named vehicles carry most of the weight. Brazil pairs Ministry of Defence R&D support with procurement to build a self-sustaining industrial base oriented toward long-term regional export; Argentina channels prototype work through its defence research programmes, which funds demonstrators but which recurring fiscal crises prevent from reaching mass procurement; Colombia routes spending through the state-owned CIAC, under the Ministry of Defence's Social and Business Defence Group, to ensure platforms are purpose-built for its asymmetric environment. Sector-specific co-financing appears where a commercial interest is directly threatened, as with Ecopetrol's co-funding of CIAC's ART Quimbaya to protect oil pipelines from ELN attack.

Counter-drone spending follows a different and less coherent logic. It is event-driven, import-dependent and technologically fragmented: Argentina imported Rafael's Drone Dome for the 2018 G20 and 2019 Youth Olympics, Colombia brought in Spanish-made Crow systems for COP16 in Cali in 2024 and withdrew them after the summit, and Brazil fielded DroneShield's DroneGun Tactical at President Lula's 2023 inauguration. Large sums follow high-profile incidents rather than a sustained programme. Colombia's allocation of 500 billion Colombian pesos for counter-drone acquisition, announced by the General Commander of the Armed Forces in September 2025, is the largest single figure in the material, and it sits alongside a candid acknowledgement from serving officers that budgets and acquisition cycles have not matched what layered C-UAS actually requires.

The buy-versus-build calculus is decided largely by price and by the absence of local alternatives. CIAC markets DRAGOM at COP 120-145 million, roughly US$30,000-36,000, explicitly undercutting imported equivalents by about 20 percent, which is the clearest domestic cost argument in the region. At the high end there is no comparable case: Brazil bought Hermes 900 airframes from 2014, added units in 2021-22 and replaced one in 2024, while Caçador production rests on a 2013 technology-cooperation agreement with IAI. No regional firm can integrate radar, RF detection, jamming, interception and sensor fusion at the level of Northrop Grumman, Leonardo, Thales, Hensoldt or Rafael.

All of this rests on an inherently fragile base. Domestic programmes depend on imported avionics, sensors and propulsion, so supply chain shocks, export restrictions or geopolitical pressure from the United States, Israel or China can stall national programmes outright, whatever the budget line says.

narrative:
The regulatory foundation for unmanned systems in Latin America rests on a single shared decision: drones are aircraft. Brazil's RBAC-E No. 94, Mexico's Norma Oficial Mexicana, Argentina's RAAC Parte 100 and Colombia's RAC 100 all define the flying component of an unmanned system as an aircraft, mirroring the United States' Title 14 CFR treatment of unmanned aircraft and sUAS. That choice is consequential rather than semantic. It places drones under civil aviation authorities with jurisdiction over licensing, certification, airworthiness and enforcement; it justifies registration, remote identification and altitude ceilings; it opens a path to harmonisation under the Chicago Convention and ICAO standards; and it allows states to criminalise unauthorised operation with penalties far heavier than consumer-law violations would carry.

On that common anchor the four surveyed states have built frameworks with recognisably similar pillars but divergent detail. Classification splits between the U.S. weight-and-kinetic-energy logic and the Latin American risk-tiered model borrowed from Europe: abierta, especifica and certificada in Argentina and Colombia, Class 3/2/1 in Brazil, micro/pequeno/grande in Mexico. Operating rules converge on a roughly 400-foot ceiling and visual line of sight as the default, with BVLOS and night flight everywhere pushed into waiver or special-authorisation territory. Airspace management is handled through fixed exclusion rings whose radii vary sharply, from Mexico's 3.7 km around aerodromes to Colombia's non-waivable 9 km around Aerodrome Reference Points, alongside protected-site regimes covering refineries, prisons, military areas and government headquarters. Personnel rules diverge most: Mexico and Colombia require medical fitness, training and civil liability insurance, while Argentina's Executive Order 550/2025 stripped licensing below 25 kg entirely.

Digital governance is where the region separates. The United States has operationalised Remote ID and LAANC nationwide. Brazil's DECEA is piloting BR-UTM; Argentina's RAAC 101 and Colombia's RAC 100 recognise Remote ID in principle; Mexico still governs mainly through registration and weight thresholds with no UTM backbone. Counter-UAS is the sharper gap. Where U.S. statute names mitigation authorities and NATO treats counter-UAS as a priority capability, Latin American practice is event-driven and import-dependent, from the Crow system at COP16 to Drone Dome at the 2018 G20.

The chapter's own verdict is that aviation-centric law, designed for accident prevention among compliant operators, cannot govern adaptive hostile actors; Colombia's draft defence bill on drones and anti-drone systems is presented as the direction of travel.

narrative:
Civilian and commercial drone use in Latin America accelerated sharply through 2025, expanding across the five domains the World Bank identified in its 2024 report Drones for Development: healthcare, agriculture, road infrastructure maintenance, reforestation and environmental monitoring, and disaster/risk management. The chapter frames itself explicitly as an update to that study rather than a replacement, arguing that the region is moving from isolated pilot projects toward more structured and impactful adoption. Brazil and Mexico lead in both scale and innovation, driving the region's most mature civilian ecosystems through BVLOS logistics pilots, public-health applications such as vector control, and medical delivery networks.

Agriculture is the clearest growth engine and delivers the most measurable productivity gains. Mexico has become the region's largest agricultural drone market: DJI has sold more than 500,000 units there since 2015 and certified over 3,000 operators through an academy founded in 2022, spray drone sales have risen 56-fold since 2016, and drone-enabled precision irrigation has cut avocado water consumption by up to 40 percent. Brazil's agribusiness sector relies heavily on DJI Agras T40 and T50 platforms, with drones halving operational costs in coffee production, while the Ministry of Agriculture has introduced operator competency standards. Argentina's uptake followed deregulation via Decrees 663/2024 and 664/2024; Colombia integrates drones steadily for crop monitoring, mapping, precision irrigation and harvest estimation, with export growth partly attributed to precision agriculture.

Maturity is uneven across the other sectors. Road infrastructure monitoring remains thin everywhere: Argentina and Brazil show scarce large-scale examples beyond private service firms such as DroneXplora and Geoscan and a proposed inspection role under Brazil's Ecovias Araguaia concession, while Mexico reports roughly 60 percent faster inspections on its National Road Network. Environmental work is more advanced, with MORFO and ReflorestaRio in Brazil, ReForest LATAM's iSeed capsules across Argentina and Brazil, Michoacan's publicly backed seed-dispersal pilots, Costa Rican wildlife tracking and Yanomami-led illegal mining monitoring. Disaster response saw drones documenting Argentina's early-2025 wildfires, University of Sao Paulo thermal and gas-sensor prototypes, Xmobots fire monitoring, and Propeller Mexico surveying 11,800 hectares in four days for flood modelling in Sonora.

Colombia is repeatedly described as comparatively limited outside agriculture, with minimal road maintenance use, only a small CIDEAL reforestation project, and largely theoretical disaster initiatives, constrained by a framing of drones primarily as security threats. Institutional capacity is now the binding constraint on moving from pilots to scalable services.

narrative:
Illicit logistics in Latin America operate across two complementary physical domains: entrenched ground routes and an expanding aerial layer of modified commercial drones. The central claim is that drones do not replace existing smuggling infrastructure but complement it, offering greater speed, stealth and flexibility in high-risk scenarios while creating new border-security challenges and alternative pathways for drugs and contraband. Mexico is the pivotal early case: from around 2015, reports described commercial drones modified to carry illicit cargo along specific routes, among the first documented uses of unmanned systems for trafficking in the region. The initial adoption by the Sinaloa Cartel, La Familia Michoacana and the CJNG was logistical rather than kinetic.

Prisons have become the most visible and chronic vulnerability node. Drone deliveries into detention facilities have been observed for more than a decade, beginning with a 2014 interception attempt at Brazil's Sao Jose dos Campos Provisional Detention Center, where roughly 250 grams of cocaine landed in the patio and inmates collected it before guards intervened. By 2019, Rio Grande do Sul authorities seized 43 drones used to move around 4 kg of narcotics and 68 mobile phones into prisons, without identifying the responsible organization. Panama's La Joya prison saw repeated November 2025 deliveries of marijuana, a cell phone, pistol parts and "crispi," and Panamanian authorities report seizing 1,587 drones used for illicit prison deliveries nationwide. The threat also comes from inside the state: seven Colombian prison guards were prosecuted in December 2021 for drone-smuggling contraband into Tramacua Prison at extortionate prices, from US$100 for fried rice to US$380 per pound of marijuana.

Ground routes remain the backbone. Cartels are most successful in the land domain, and the U.S.-Mexico border is the primary entry point for cocaine, marijuana, heroin and methamphetamine. Tunnels, concealed shipments in vehicles and trucks amid overwhelming inspection volumes, and human couriers persist because they move tons rather than kilograms, face fewer payload limits, and exploit entrenched infrastructure at low cost once routes are secured.

Aerial capacity is therefore specialized rather than substitutive: modified drones carry only a few kilograms, suiting high-value, low-weight cargo or tactical missions, while eliminating human traces, improving accuracy and evading radar. Escalation is evident in reconnaissance, command-and-control, bombing and propaganda uses, culminating in April 2024 when CJNG drones dropped explosive devices filled with chemical substances over Michoacan, causing respiratory distress and marking the first known cartel use of chemical weapons.

items.label: Complement, not replacement

outline.heading: Prison smuggling: drones behind the walls

items.label: A decade-old, region-wide pattern
items.detail: Drone delivery of contraband into prisons has become increasingly frequent across Latin America and has been observed for more than a decade, making prisons a chronic vulnerability node.

items.label: The threat from inside the state
items.detail: Drone-enabled prison smuggling is not exclusively a criminal-organization activity; prison staff themselves have been implicated, meaning the vulnerability is partly institutional rather than purely technological.

outline.heading: Ground routes: the backbone of trafficking

items.label: Land remains the core domain
items.detail: As Sean Harney argues, cartels are most successful in the land domain, which remains the core of their smuggling operations; trafficking organizations run flexible systems integrating traditional ground routes with emerging drone capacity.

items.label: Why ground methods persist
items.detail: They move tons rather than kilograms, face fewer payload restrictions than aerial methods, and benefit from entrenched infrastructure and relatively low costs once routes are secured.

items.label: Exploiting surveillance gaps
items.detail: Flexible ground-plus-air logistics systems are designed around persistent weaknesses in state surveillance rather than around any single technology.

items.label: Short-lived test platforms
items.detail: Harney underscores that drones do not replace traditional smuggling routes; they serve as complementary, short-lived test platforms expanding operational flexibility alongside established infrastructure.

items.label: Erosion of state control over airspace and borders
items.detail: Drone adoption represents a structural shift in power, undermining conventional enforcement in areas already under heavy surveillance and patrol and leaving institutions behind faster-innovating criminal networks.

items.label: Response requires layered counter-drone defense
items.detail: A sustainable answer needs layered counter-drone defenses combined with interagency coordination and international cooperation, rather than ad hoc technological fixes; without reform states remain reactive and dependent on foreign solutions.

narrative:
Argentina's fleet is state-led and largely domestic, but only a few systems are genuinely fielded. The Lipan M3, begun in the mid-1990s, is the mainstay: 60 kg MTOW, 20 kg payload, operational since 2014 and reportedly exported to Egypt. The AR-1F Buho trainer, roughly 10 km range and 40 minutes endurance, reached the Air Force in 2021, while the heavier AR-1A Aukan, about 100 kg MTOW and four hours endurance, is still in testing.

Everything more ambitious remains unproven. Argentina's Vigia 2B MALE concept, a 12 m wingspan design with MTOW above 1,000 kg, 14 hours endurance and range approaching 2,000 km, has no announced prototype, and the RUAS-160 coaxial rotorcraft is a prototype. The Navy's PIELAGOS and the Army's VAE/VAD ground vehicles are in development. Counter-UAS is imported: Rafael's Drone Dome covered the 2018 G20 and the Youth Olympics.

Argentine unmanned development, including unmanned ground vehicles, is financed at prototype rather than fleet scale. narrative:
Argentina's RAAC Parte 100 treats a remotely piloted vehicle as an aircraft flown from a remote control station, and sorts operations strictly by weight and risk rather than purpose: abierta at 25 kg MTOW or less with optional registration, especifica from 25 to 150 kg requiring authorisation, and certificada above 150 kg requiring aircraft certification. Flights are capped at 46-61 m AGL, must stay 3 NM from aerodrome runway thresholds and 1 NM from heliports, night operations are broadly restricted, and overflying crowds is prohibited without approval.

RAAC 101 recognises Remote ID as an integration prerequisite and the 2025 rules call for a UTM system. Executive Order 550/2025 repealed the earlier UAV regulation, ending oversight below 250 g, licensing up to 25 kg, and one firm's training monopoly. Liability rests with the exploiter; security forces may terminate noncompliant flights.

outline.heading: UAVs as aircraft: the common regulatory anchor

items.label: Remotely piloted vehicle defined as aircraft
items.detail: Argentina's RAAC Parte 100 defines a remotely piloted vehicle as an aircraft intended to fly without a pilot on board and piloted from a remote control station, with RPAS as the configurable set of elements integrated around it.

items.label: Abierta / especifica / certificada
items.detail: Argentina defines abierta at 25 kg MTOW or less with optional registration, especifica at 25-150 kg requiring authorisation, and certificada above 150 kg requiring aircraft certification, classifying strictly by weight and risk without distinguishing purpose of use.

outline.heading: Operational limitations: altitude, visibility and night flight

items.label: Night flight broadly restricted
items.detail: Night operations are broadly restricted or prohibited in Argentina, with permission granted only on explicit technical approval and formal authorisation.

outline.heading: Airspace management: airport proximity, protected facilities and overflight of people

items.label: Hierarchical aerodrome and heliport limits
items.detail: Argentina limits RPAS to 46-61 m (150-200 ft) AGL and requires them to remain outside a 3 NM radius from an aerodrome runway threshold and 1 NM from heliports, distinguishing controlled from uncontrolled airspace; operations inside those limits need Air Navigation Service Provider authorisation.

items.label: Prohibition on overflying crowds
items.detail: Under the latest Argentine regulations, RPAS overflight of crowds or agglomerations of people is prohibited unless specifically approved by the aeronautical authority.

items.label: Remote ID recognised as an integration prerequisite
items.detail: Argentina's RAAC 101 formally recognises Remote ID as a prerequisite for safe and efficient RPAS integration, and the latest 2025 regulations call for a UTM system to manage drone operations in an integrated airspace.

items.label: Executive Order 550/2025 deregulation
items.detail: President Javier Milei's executive order repealed the Reglamento de Vehiculos Aereos no Tripulados y Sistemas de Vehiculos Aereos no Tripulados, removing state oversight for drones under 250 g and eliminating licensing for drones up to 25 kg to stimulate agriculture, commerce, medicine delivery and border security; it also dismantled one company's monopoly on drone training, opening the field to all qualified instructors and training centres. The chapter's text dates the order to 2005, evidently a typographical error for 2025.

items.label: Exploiter liability and tiered insurance
items.detail: Under RAAC provisions responsibility for RPAS operation lies with the exploiter, whether owner or third party, including liability for damage to persons and property; abierta operators are exempt from insurance while especifica and certificada operators must obtain coverage scaled to weight class as determined by the competent authority.

items.label: Security force intervention powers
items.detail: Argentina grants explicit authority to military, police and security forces to intervene in or terminate unauthorised or noncompliant drone operations; interference with or inhibition of RPAS signals by unauthorised third parties is prohibited, with an exception for security forces acting lawfully, and RPA operators must obey orders from security personnel. The Argentine Aeronautical Authority may define No Drone Zones where operations are prohibited, and security forces may be called on to enforce compliance.

narrative:
Civilian uptake is real but shallow. The medical drone market is valued at roughly US$5 million, yet evidence of large-scale operational use stays limited compared with Brazil, with few initiatives recorded in 2025. Agriculture is the most improved segment: Decrees 663/2024 and 664/2024 stripped out dated bureaucratic barriers, a reform DJI welcomed, and a May 2025 event at the Estacion Experimental Rufino Mir and the Agencia de Extension Rural 25 de Mayo put producers and contractors in front of the platforms, one participant describing drones as complementing existing technology at specific sites.

Infrastructure work remains niche, with DroneXplora offering topography, orthomosaics and volumetric calculations but few large road-maintenance applications. Drone footage of the early-2025 wildfires in central Argentina and Patagonia reached international outlets and the Global Wildfire Information System.

narrative:
Brazil fields the region's deepest unmanned inventory. The Air Force has flown Elbit's Hermes 900 (RQ-900), supplied through AEL Sistemas of Porto Alegre, since 2014, adding units in 2021-22 and a 2024 replacement after a loss, for homeland security and Amazon monitoring. Avionics Services builds the Cacador from IAI's Heron-1 under a 2013 agreement, while Stella Tecnologia's Atoba (500 kg, 11 m span, 28 hours) and the armed Condor give Brazil the region's only domestic hunter-killer roadmap.

Below that sit Xmobots' Nauru 1000C, under Army evaluation for border surveillance, and the Nauru 500C used against illegal mining in 2024; Stella's ship-capable Albatroz; SantosLab's Carcara and FT Sistemas' FT-100 Horus. NEST's ATD-150 jet target drone flew in June 2025. Ground and naval work covers the Marine Corps' Robo Expedicionario UGV and the EMGEPRON-TideWise Suppressor USV. Counter-drone systems span IACIT's DRONEBlocker, the Army's SCE-0100 and imported DroneGun Tactical jammers.

narrative:
Brazil is the only Latin American country with a comprehensive drone industrial base, spanning military, civilian and counter-drone production. Stella Tecnologia covers the MALE segment with the Atoba, the Condor hunter-killer and the naval Albatroz; Xmobots supplies the Army's Nauru 1000C and 500C and has pursued an armed roadmap with MBDA; SantosLab, FT Sistemas and Avibras deliver small tactical ISR platforms; SkyDrones concentrates on civilian and dual-use work. NEST Design Aerospace built the ATD-150, Brazil's first fully indigenous jet-powered UAV.

Foreign technology remains woven in: AEL Sistemas supplies the Hermes 900, Avionics Services produces the Cacador under a 2013 IAI agreement, and the Embraer-AEL Harpia venture fielded the Hermes 450 before closing in 2016. Naval and ground segments trail the air segment, with EMGEPRON and TideWise's Suppressor USV the bellwether. IACIT, the Army's SCE-0100, the BIRDS consortium and DECEA's BR-UTM anchor the counter-drone and traffic-management layer.

narrative:
Israel is Brazil's dominant external supplier. narrative:
Brazil's RBAC-E No. 94 classifies unmanned aerial vehicles as aircraft, specifically remotely piloted aircraft flown from a remote pilot station for any purpose other than recreation. Brazil is unique in the region for a purpose-first split between recreational aeromodelos and RPAs, with weight thresholds layering on further burdens: Class 3 up to 25 kg, Class 2 from 25 to 150 kg and Class 1 above 150 kg.

Airspace governance is shared between ANAC and DECEA, which applies Flight Restriction Zones. Drones up to 25 kg face graduated altitude and speed rings around aerodromes, and refineries, fuel depots, prisons, military areas, government headquarters, utilities, dams and air-navigation networks may not be overflown without authorisation. People are classed as involved, consenting or nonconsenting, with overflight of the last prohibited absent ANAC airworthiness certification. DECEA has launched BR-UTM and can suspend operations, request police seizure and pursue criminal penalties.

outline.heading: Airspace management: airport proximity, protected facilities and overflight of people

items.label: Dual ANAC/DECEA airspace governance
items.detail: Brazil splits airspace management between the National Civil Aviation Agency (ANAC) and the Department of Airspace Control (DECEA), with DECEA applying the Flight Restriction Zone concept to protect critical areas; access near aerodromes requires airport operator authorisation and operations must cease immediately when manned aircraft approach.

items.label: Graduated rings around aerodromes and heliports
items.detail: For drones up to 25 kg MTOW Brazil caps operations at 100 ft AGL and 30 knots within 1,740 m of aerodromes or heliports, 100-200 ft and 60 knots within 2,350 m, and 300-400 ft and 60 knots within 3,570 m.

items.label: Designated areas of security
items.detail: Brazil heavily restricts operations over critical national infrastructure and security installations including refineries, fuel depots, penal establishments, military areas, government headquarters, water and gas supply networks, dams, and communication and air navigation surveillance networks, none of which may be overflown without prior authorisation from the responsible authorities.

items.label: Three categories of persons on the surface
items.detail: Brazil mandates operations in areas distant from third parties and classifies people as persons involved in the operation, consenting persons who accept the risk, and uninvolved or nonconsenting persons, over whom overflight is prohibited. Flying above populated areas or nonconsenting crowds in Brazil is conditional on certification of the entire system, specifically an airworthiness certificate issued by ANAC; microdrones under 250 g may operate over people and are exempt from ANAC registration.

items.detail: Brazilian regulations provide for neutralisation of threats, particularly overflight of sensitive or restricted areas, and empower DECEA to suspend any operation deemed necessary to maintain safety; the aeronautical authority may request police assistance to detain presumed offenders or seize aircraft endangering public safety, with criminal charges and administrative penalties available.

narrative:
Brazil's civilian sector is among the region's most mature. In healthcare, AMVP Saude works with the Public Health Secretariat of Minas Gerais on drone-based vector control against Zika, Chikungunya and Dengue, reaching roofs, slabs and abandoned parcels otherwise inaccessible. Speedbird Aero has consolidated its position as the leading delivery operator, flying pioneering logistics missions with Vale and expanding beyond BVLOS drone-port infrastructure. Agriculture is the largest driver, with DJI's Agras T40 and T50 widely used for spraying and crop monitoring, operational costs halved in coffee production, and the Agriculture Ministry setting operator competency standards.

Infrastructure monitoring lags: a 2025 proposal by the terrestrial transport agency would add drones to road inspections under the Ecovias Araguaia concession, and Geoscan offers LiDAR services. Environmental and disaster work is stronger, spanning MORFO's ReflorestaRio monitoring, Paragominas seed-dispersal pilots, Yanomami-led illegal mining monitoring, USP fire-detection prototypes and Xmobots fire response.

narrative:
Brazil's documented illicit drone logistics centre on prisons. In 2014, authorities at the Sao Jose dos Campos Provisional Detention Center tried to intercept a drone carrying roughly 250 grams of cocaine; the package was dropped into the patio and inmates collected it before guards could intervene.

The scale became clearer in 2019, when law enforcement in Rio Grande do Sul seized 43 drones used to smuggle around 4 kg of narcotics and 68 mobile phones into prison facilities. Despite the size of that operation, authorities could not identify the criminal organisation behind it, leaving the network structure unresolved. Together the two cases show contraband delivery over prison walls as the established Brazilian pattern, distinct from the battlefield-style drone use documented elsewhere in the region.

narrative:
Colombia's fielded inventory is state-owned and sits at the tactical and small-tactical tiers. CIAC's ART Quimbaya, built on a technology transfer from Spain's Aertec TARSIS-75, has a 5.24 m wingspan, 74 kg MTOW, 7 kg payload, 8-10 hours endurance and 100 km range; it was delivered to the Air Force in 2021 and co-financed by Ecopetrol to protect pipelines from ELN attack. Below it sit the DRAGOM multirotor, unveiled in 2025 with 75-90 minutes endurance, 6-10 kg payload and a cited latent mortar or grenade attack profile, and the 5 kg hand-launched Coelum, which gained an optional VTOL configuration by Expodefensa 2023.

Counter-UAS is imported. Police and military field the U.S.-made Dronebuster, and Spain's Crow system protected COP16 in Cali in 2024, detecting over 300 drones and neutralising 90 unauthorised flights before being withdrawn after the summit.

narrative:
The ELN, FARC dissidents who rejected the 2016 peace agreement, and post-2016 criminal structures have folded drones into the five pillars of guerrilla warfare, becoming 'techno guerrillas' with a more offensive posture against civilians, soldiers, vehicles and bases. Modified commercial DJI quadcopters dropping grenades are the dominant attack mode. Interviews indicate roughly 230 drone-enabled attacks since June 2024; Semana documented 313 explosive attacks between April 2024 and 31 August 2025, involving some 713 grenades and 215 killed and wounded.

Colombian Air Force officers report continual adaptation: new flight profiles, longer battery endurance, night operations and modifications designed to evade common jammers. Groups learn from YouTube and TikTok tutorials, observation of Ukraine and Syria and sometimes direct external instruction, and have folded UAS into trafficking and illegal mining.

items.label: Improvised munitions drops / bomb-droppers

items.label: Psychological operations and propaganda

items.label: Illicit economy integration
items.detail: UAS capabilities have been folded into trafficking, illegal mining and other revenue-generating operations, increasing both operational reach and the financial resiliency of armed groups.

items.detail: Colombian insurgents appear to have mimicked Ukrainian tactics by modifying commercial drones to extend reach, increase lethality and reinforce psychological intimidation, driving a spike in violence and previously unseen forms of attack.

narrative:
Colombia's unmanned sector is overwhelmingly state-owned and defence-led, centred on CIAC, which operates under the Ministry of Defence's Social and Business Defence Group and combines in-house R&D, fabrication and operational integration across the air force, army and navy, with the stated goal of reducing foreign dependence. Its portfolio is the DRAGOM multirotor, designed and built entirely in Colombia and marketed at COP 120-145 million (about US$30,000-36,000), roughly 20 percent below imports; the 5 kg Coelum; and the ART Quimbaya. CODALTEC adds ISR platforms and command-and-control systems.

Scale is the weakness. Quimbaya lost prototype X-004 in 2022 and its limited fielding suggests a pilot programme rather than mass production. There is no domestic counter-UAS industry: police and military rely on imports such as the Dronebuster.

narrative:
Colombia's drone landscape is shaped by three external sources. Chinese commercial retail supplies the threat: FARC dissidents and ELN factions have incorporated the DJI Mavic for reconnaissance, surveillance of military positions and monitoring of strategic corridors, and Colombian authorities have documented more than 300 drone-enabled attacks in recent years, with open-source video confirming recurring Mavic involvement.

The state side depends on Europe and the United States. CIAC's ART Quimbaya rests on a technology transfer from Spain's Aertec TARSIS-75, was co-financed by Ecopetrol to protect oil pipelines under ELN threat and was delivered to the Air Force in 2021 for border surveillance, counternarcotics and illegal mining interdiction. Counter-drone capability is procured abroad, notably the U.S.-made Dronebuster.

narrative:
Colombian funding is state-led and announced faster than it is executed. On 26 September 2025 Admiral Francisco Cubides Granados said the government had allocated COP 500 billion for counter-drone acquisition to protect military bases and critical infrastructure, alongside designated army drone battalions and research into domestic counter-UAS. Earlier, state oil company Ecopetrol co-financed CIAC's ART Quimbaya to protect pipelines under ELN threat, delivered in 2021, and CIAC prices DRAGOM roughly 20 percent below imports as its build-versus-buy argument.

Execution lags. Senior officers cite procurement cycles, budget shortfalls and delays as the core reason doctrine outruns capability; the imported Crow systems used at COP16 in Cali left no residual capability. Contested Skies II recommends an acceleration programme modelled on Ukraine's Brave1.

narrative:
Colombia regulates drones through RAC 100, whose preamble affirms that the flying components of unmanned aircraft systems are aircraft and therefore subject to the Aeronautical Regulations of Colombia. It applies three tiers: abierta for noncommercial drones of 25 kg or less, especifica for commercial or heavier operations up to 250 kg, and certificada for manned-equivalent systems, still unauthorised pending ICAO standards. VLOS is capped at 750 metres, extendable to 3 km with observers; Open Category flights are barred within 9 km of aerodrome reference points and 3 km of heliports, and 30 metres from unassociated persons and buildings.

All drones over 200 grams must be registered, especifica requires a certificado de idoneidad and insurance, and police may confiscate drones. A Defence Ministry bill would add registries and harsher penalties for terrorist drone use.

items.detail: Colombian regulations empower the police to halt, control and confiscate drones using available technological means where operations infringe regulations or pose an imminent threat to public safety; in cases of grave or imminent risk the competent authority may take preventive measures and suspend pilot privileges.

narrative:
Colombia's civilian adoption is uneven and mostly early-stage. Agriculture is the exception: drones are steadily integrated for crop monitoring, pesticide distribution, terrain mapping, precision irrigation and harvest estimation, and studies attribute part of the rise in agricultural exports since 2020 to precision agriculture and drone use. Retail chains such as Agrowtek distribute DJI products at scale, embedding drones in established farming supply networks.

Elsewhere progress is thin. Medical drone transport remained limited as of September 2025, though start-ups such as Orkid S.A.S., supported by Aeronautica Civil's drone and urban aerial mobility group, are beginning to carry medicines and laboratory samples. Road maintenance use is minimal, environmental work is confined to a small CIDEAL reforestation project in Madrid, Cundinamarca benefiting 67 productive units, and disaster initiatives remain largely theoretical.

narrative:
Colombia's documented drone logistics problem is contraband delivery into prisons, enabled by insider collusion. In December 2021 seven guards of the National Penitentiary and Prison Institute were prosecuted for using drones to smuggle food, alcohol, electronics, drugs and cell phones into Tramacua Prison in Valledupar.

Prosecutor Juan Carlos Linero reported that the guards charged exorbitant prices for what they flew in: around US$100 for a portion of fried rice, US$250 for alcohol, US$380 per pound of marijuana and up to US$500 for other drugs. The case shows drones serving as the delivery mechanism for an established internal market, with staff participation setting the terms of supply.

narrative:
Mexico's domestic line is essentially Hydra Technologies' family, marketed and demonstrated regionally for civil and security roles; Contested Skies I could not independently verify combat employment of any of them. The G3 Guerrero (4.06 m wingspan, 9-10 hours, ~4 kg payload) serves police and military surveillance and mapping, alongside the S4 Ehecatl (9.5 m, ~8 hours, 45 kg payload) and the twin-engine S45 Baalam (6.11 m, up to 12 hours), which flew a first demonstration in Guatemala. The larger S50 Kukulkan (7.68 m, up to 16 hours, ~25 kg) is reported rather than confirmed.

Above them sits the S55 Ares, a MALE-class twin-engine design in development for ISR, ELINT/SIGINT, maritime patrol and ground attack at up to 22 hours endurance, ~160 km range with optional satcom BLOS and an 18,500 ft ceiling; its guided-munition capability remains an unverified vendor claim. The Navy's SPARTAAM programme, an indigenous ship-integrated patrol capability for maritime domain awareness, coastal surveillance and search and rescue, has few confirmed timelines.

narrative:
Mexican cartels use commercial UAS for reconnaissance, smuggling and offensive operations, exploiting open-source training and foreign contacts to refine tactics and adapting to countermeasures faster than the state responds. The CJNG, the Sinaloa Cartel and La Familia Michoacana are each named as modifying commercial systems to deliver explosives and, in a recent escalation, chemical agents, complementing ground routes with speed, stealth and flexibility. The CJNG also uses cryptocurrency to procure weapons and drones.

The contest has become two-sided: cartels have acquired their own counter-UAS systems to neutralise rivals' drones, producing a criminal arms race in which non-state actors both operate and defend against unmanned systems. Transnational criminal organizations have reportedly embedded personnel in foreign conflict theatres for hands-on training in battlefield drone innovation, creating a temporal asymmetry against state forces following simplified manuals.

narrative:
Mexico's industry is a hybrid of private manufacturing and military-led R&D. Hydra Technologies anchors it with a marketed line spanning the G3 Guerrero, S4 Ehecatl, S45 Baalam, S50 Kukulkan and the aspirational MALE-class S55 Ares, oriented to policing, coastal, maritime and border surveillance. Its weaponization claims require verification, particularly given SEDENA's statutory monopoly on arms production and export. AV3 Aerovisual works the dual-use surveillance, security and commercial market instead of Hydra's military line.

On the state side, SEMAR is developing SPARTAAM, a ship-integrated ISR programme built with naval research units and national partners, while SEDENA pursues prototypes with national research institutions and the Secretariat of Science, Humanities, Technology and Innovation. Counter-UAS is the clear gap: Mexico has no meaningful domestic C-UAS industry and buys predominantly from foreign vendors such as NQ Defense.

narrative:
Mexico's external dependence runs through two very different channels. On the commercial side, China's DJI Mavic - affordable, compact and easy to fly - is the most frequently repurposed platform by non-state actors, and the CJNG and La Familia Michoacana have used it for surveillance of security forces, ambush coordination and, in some cases, IED delivery. That diffusion arrives through ordinary retail rather than any controlled procurement route.

On the state side, the dependence is defensive. With no meaningful domestic counter-UAS industry, the counter-drone systems deployed by Mexican authorities and private customers are predominantly purchased abroad through official procurement, with vendors such as NQ Defense reporting deliveries; the supplier country is not stated in the source material.

narrative:
Mexico's Norma Oficial Mexicana treats an unmanned aircraft as an aircraft meant to be operated without a pilot on board, with RPAS one type of uncrewed aircraft, aiming at operations harmonised with manned aviation. It sorts systems by weight - micro at 2 kg or less, pequeno above 2 kg to 25 kg, grande above 25 kg - without formally separating recreational from professional use, and requires registration of anything over 250 grams with AFAC, which replaced the DGAC in October 2019.

Airspace rules are strict: no operation within 3.7 km of aerodromes, 30-100 m caps and special authorisation out to 18.5 km, 122 m elsewhere for micro and small RPAS, and graduated limits on overflying people. Operators need an autorizacion or licencia valid three years, plus civil liability insurance for all non-recreational flights. No UTM system has been operationalised.

items.label: Aerodrome exclusion and graduated caps
items.detail: Mexico prohibits operation of all RPAS classes within 3.7 km (2 NM) of aerodromes; between 3.7 and 18.5 km operating height is capped at 30-100 m and both commercial and noncommercial flights require special authorisation. Mexican RPAS operations are barred in prohibited, restricted or dangerous areas designated by the competent authority; outside airport and heliport zones micro and small RPAS are capped at 122 m (400 ft). Mexico sets an absolute prohibition within 0.2 km (0.1 NM) of heliports and altitude caps of 30-50 m between 0.2 km and 0.9 km, with special authorisation required for commercial and private noncommercial flights.

items.label: Overflight of people by class
items.detail: Micro RPAS may overfly people; small RPAS may only overfly persons directly participating and must keep a 30-50 m perimeter from unrelated persons depending on weight; large RPAS may not overfly non-participants and must keep a 50 m buffer, with special authorisation from the Aeronautical Authority required to fly over nonparticipating persons.

items.detail: Mexico continues to regulate primarily through registration and weight-based restrictions and has not yet operationalised a UTM system.

items.label: Autorizacion and licencia
items.detail: Mexico distinguishes an autorizacion for small/pequeno RPAS from a licencia for large/grande systems, each valid three years, contingent on specific courses and minimum flight hours, and both requiring proof of medical fitness and a minimum age of 18. Recreational use in Mexico requires no specific licence but must occur within aeromodelling clubs authorised by the aviation authority; micro RPAS are exempt from pilot certification for recreational purposes, though any RPAS over 0.25 kg must be registered.

items.label: Mandatory civil liability insurance
items.detail: Mexico mandates civil liability insurance for all commercial and private noncommercial operations regardless of RPAS size, with no insurance required for strictly recreational use.

narrative:
Mexico is the region's largest agricultural drone market. More than 500,000 DJI units have sold since 2015 and over 3,000 operators have been certified through the training academy founded in 2022, with DJI adding the Agras T100, T70P and T25P in 2025. Spray drone sales have risen 56-fold since 2016, and avocado farming has cut water consumption by up to 40 percent through drone-enabled precision irrigation.

Health and public-sector uses are scaling too: large-scale medical trials and operations were underway by 2025, driven by the need to reach Indigenous communities in remote rural regions, with multi-rotor drones moving supplies between urban hospitals. Road inspections cut inspection times by roughly 60 percent despite otherwise limited uptake, Michoacan piloted pre-germinated seed distribution over wildfire-affected forests, and Propeller Mexico surveyed about 11,800 hectares in Ciudad Obregon, Sonora, in four days for flood-prevention modelling.

items.label: Spray drone diffusion and water savings
items.detail: Spray drone sales increased 56-fold since 2016, and avocado farming reduced water consumption by up to 40 percent through drone-enabled precision irrigation.

items.label: National Road Network inspections

items.detail: State authorities launched pilots to distribute pre-germinated seeds across wildfire-affected forests; media reports detailed payloads, germination rates and coverage, confirming the official nature of the operations, with France24 video footage showing drones dispersing seeds in the field.

narrative:
Mexico was one of the earliest contexts anywhere in which criminal groups adapted commercial drones - not to attack rivals or police, but to move product. Reports from around 2015 described drones modified to carry illicit cargo along specific routes, with the Sinaloa Cartel, La Familia Michoacana and the CJNG all adopting them as logistical tools before any tactical use. Aerial movement complements the ground backbone of the U.S.-Mexico border - tunnels, concealed vehicle and truck shipments, and human couriers - offering speed and stealth at only a few kilograms per load, eliminating human traces, improving accuracy and evading radar.

Use then escalated into reconnaissance and command-and-control during confrontations, aerial bombings, direct assaults and propaganda. In April 2024 the CJNG dropped explosive devices filled with chemical substances over Michoacan, causing respiratory distress - the first known cartel use of chemical weapons.

outline.heading: Drones and the evolution of illicit logistics

items.label: Mexico as the earliest adopter
items.detail: Mexico stands out as one of the earliest contexts in which criminal groups adapted commercial drones, not to attack law enforcement or rivals but to facilitate drug trafficking. Reports from around 2015 described drones modified to carry illicit cargo across specific routes.

items.label: Logistics-first adoption by three cartels
items.detail: Initial adoption by the Sinaloa Cartel, La Familia Michoacana (LFM) and the CJNG focused specifically on using drones as logistical tools for transporting narcotics, before any tactical or offensive use.

outline.heading: Ground routes: the backbone of trafficking

items.label: U.S.-Mexico border as primary entry point
items.detail: The border serves as the primary entry point for illicit drugs into the United States, including cocaine, marijuana, heroin and methamphetamine.

items.label: Underground tunnels
items.detail: Tunnels bypass surface-level detection entirely and form one of the three principal land-based smuggling methods described.

items.label: Concealed vehicle and truck shipments
items.detail: Shipments hidden in vehicles and trucks exploit crossings where inspection volumes are overwhelming, balancing risk against efficiency.

items.label: Human couriers or "mules"
items.detail: Couriers carry smaller quantities on their bodies, providing a low-signature complement to bulk vehicle and tunnel movement.

items.label: Speed and stealth at low payload
items.detail: The aerial domain offers speed and stealth but limited capacity. CJNG, Sinaloa Cartel and LFM have modified commercial drones typically able to carry only a few kilograms, unsuitable for bulk but ideal for high-value, low-weight contraband or tactical missions.

items.label: Operational advantages beyond cost
items.detail: Drones eliminate human traces, increase delivery accuracy, and evade radar in areas already subject to ground patrols.

items.label: Airspace penetration for intelligence
items.detail: Mexican cartels use drones for reconnaissance, surveillance and command-and-control during confrontations with rival cartels, state security forces and local self-defense groups, in direct support of illicit logistics.

items.label: Offensive and psychological uses
items.detail: Drones have been adapted for aerial bombings, direct assaults, and operations tied to propaganda and psychological warfare.

items.label: Chemical payloads over Michoacan (April 2024)
items.detail: The CJNG deployed drones carrying explosive devices filled with chemical substances; residents reported gases causing respiratory distress, marking the first known use of chemical weapons by a cartel.

items.label: Trajectory toward greater lethality
items.detail: The Michoacan case signals a potential trajectory toward increasingly lethal tactics, given the accessibility of commercial drones and the relative ease of modifying them into improvised weapons.

outline.heading: Prison smuggling: drones behind the walls

items.label: La Joya prison, Panama (Nov 2025)
items.detail: Per InSight Crime, two drones delivered marijuana and a cell phone on 12 November 2025; three days later another dropped pistol parts and narcotics; on 22 November a further drone carried a package of "crispi," a mixture of coca leaves and marijuana.

items.label: Weapons parts entering by air
items.detail: The 15 November 2025 La Joya delivery included pistol parts alongside narcotics, showing drone payloads extending beyond drugs and phones into firearm components.

items.label: Scale of Panamanian seizures
items.detail: Panamanian authorities have reported seizing 1,587 drones used for illicit deliveries across the country's prisons, underscoring the scale and persistence of the problem.

narrative:
Venezuela fielded no meaningful unmanned capability until the early 2000s, yet by 2025 it had assembled one of the region's most diverse arsenals. The ANSU-100 (Arpia), a Mohajer-2 derivative, is described as the first weaponized drone in Latin America and is assessed to carry Iranian Qaem precision-guided munitions. The Antonio Jose de Sucre-100, modernised with Iranian support, conducts reconnaissance and anti-tank and anti-personnel strikes using Russian-made guided munitions. Imported platforms include Iran's Mohajer-6, supplied since 2020 to protect strategic areas, and Russia's Orlan-10, used for border surveillance and artillery fire correction.

Newer entries remain unproven. The ANSU-200 flying wing displayed in 2022 claims stealth characteristics and a strike, air-defence-suppression and counter-drone mission set; the Antonio Jose de Sucre-200 and the ANT-3X Gavilan surveillance and training platform are experimental. The Zamora V-1, a Shahed-136-derived loitering munition introduced in 2024, signals a shift toward expendable kamikaze strike.

narrative:
Venezuela's unmanned sector is a state programme rather than an industry. Operational systems carry national designations - ANSU-100 (Arpia), Antonio Jose de Sucre-100, Zamora V-1 - but their lineage is foreign: the Mohajer-2, Iranian Qaem munitions, Russian guided ordnance and the Shahed-136. Prototypes such as the ANSU-200 flying wing, the Antonio Jose de Sucre-200 and the ANT-3X Gavilan, the last intended for light surveillance and as a training tool for engineers, show ambition beyond demonstrated production.

Having fielded no meaningful capability until the early 2000s, Caracas reached this position by 2025 through more than two decades of cooperation with Iran and, to a lesser degree, Russia, supplemented by direct imports of the Mohajer-6 and Orlan-10 from 2020. The result reflects strategic partnerships and local assembly rather than domestic innovation or an indigenous industrial base.

narrative:
External suppliers, not domestic industry, built Venezuela's arsenal. Iran is the principal partner: it transferred the Mohajer-6 from 2020, backed the ANSU-100 Arpia and ANSU-200, supported the Antonio Jose de Sucre-100 and -200, and provided the Shahed-136 lineage behind the Zamora V-1. Iranian Qaem precision-guided munitions are identified as the critical escalation in lethality and the clearest marker of outside actors shaping the arsenal. Reporting from 2023 named Venezuela, alongside Bolivia, Cuba and Nicaragua, as a potential Iranian export partner.

Russia's role is smaller but formalising. The Orlan-10 has been in service since 2020 for border surveillance, target identification and artillery correction, and Russian-made guided munitions arm an Iranian-supported airframe. In September 2025 Caracas approved a bilateral pact covering security, defence and technological cooperation, framed by lawmakers as advancing a multipolar order against imperialist hegemony.

narrative:
Venezuela's case shows capability bought through alignment rather than funded through industry. From near-zero unmanned capability in the early 2000s, Caracas assembled one of the region's most diverse arsenals by 2025 on the back of more than two decades of cooperation with Iran and, to a lesser degree, Russia. No comparable domestic industrial investment underpins it, which is treated as evidence that regional balance is increasingly decoupled from local defence budgets.

The September 2025 bilateral pact with Russia, approved in Caracas and covering security, defence and technological cooperation, formalises this substitution. Framed by lawmakers as a rejection of imperialist hegemony and as advancing a multipolar order, it channels defence technology transfers outside regional export-control frameworks, meaning the inputs to Venezuela's arsenal arrive by state agreement rather than through procurement budgets or a commercial supplier base.

items.label: Large-drone export controls are weakening
items.detail: Looser interpretations by major suppliers and the U.S. reclassification of MALE systems are likely to accelerate global dissemination and lower the political and operational barriers to drone warfare.

items.label: Small-drone diffusion is effectively ungoverned
items.detail: Fragmented regulations, permissive legal environments and the absence of a coherent international regime leave sub-2 kg systems widely accessible and easily weaponized.

items.label: Missile Technology Control Regime (MTCR)
items.detail: The U.S. previously led efforts to prevent the spread of large systems under the MTCR, which presumed export denial; as a result the U.S. proliferated sophisticated UAS technology to only a handful of countries.

items.label: Escalatory risk of eased exports
items.detail: The policy shift will likely accelerate global dissemination and could fuel a cycle in which greater access to unmanned systems lowers the perceived cost of conflict, making military options more attractive than peaceful resolution.

items.label: Absent international legal regime for battlefield use
items.detail: A coherent international legal regime governing battlefield drone use is effectively nonexistent; the Hague and Geneva Conventions predate robotics and remote warfare and leave normative and procedural gaps.

items.label: Norm evolution theory
items.detail: Great powers rarely impose constraints on technologies that advance their strategic interests, instead maintaining an unrestricted posture that gradually normalizes permissive practices; new binding rules are judged unlikely.

items.label: First choice of nonstate actors
items.detail: DJI insists its drones are meant for civilian use only, yet most nonstate actors incorporating drones into drug trafficking, terrorism or armed confrontation have turned first and foremost to DJI equipment, and its models span hundreds of drones of every size, purpose and price range.

items.label: Dominance of early conflict phases
items.detail: Commercial DJI drones often dominate the initial stages of conflicts, as at the onset of the Russia-Ukraine war, owing to wide availability, simple operation and low cost; in Colombia most VNSA drones are modified DJI systems, a pattern likely to persist until widespread adoption of FPV drones assembled from cheap components or sourced through black-market flows from Russia and Ukraine.

items.label: DJI Matrice 400
items.detail: A relatively new entry with roughly one hour of endurance, higher sustained speeds, up to 6 kg payload, advanced autonomy and high-resolution optical sensors; suited to search and rescue in hostile environments including night and adverse maritime conditions.

items.label: DJI Mavic
items.detail: DJI's most iconic and widely deployed model: affordable, compact, lightweight, agile, with an intuitive control interface, steadily improving imaging and a modular architecture for accessories, making it the most frequently repurposed drone by nonstate actors.

items.label: DJI Dock 3
items.detail: Advances autonomy, endurance and environmental resilience: operates from -22F to 122F, in heavy rain and winds up to 12 m/s, with a fully autonomous docking station mountable on fixed infrastructure or vehicles and a camera generating 3D maps through iterative overflights.

items.label: DJI FPV 2
items.detail: Part of DJI's first-person-view line, flown through goggles for an immersive cockpit perspective; originally for high-speed racing but repurposed by some conflict actors toward kamikaze-style strikes.

items.label: Capability gains cut both ways
items.detail: Each year drones gain endurance, resistance to extreme temperatures, wind tolerance and weatherproofing, making them indispensable in mining, agriculture and search-and-rescue while simultaneously becoming more effective weapons.

items.label: Sophistication attracts armed groups
items.detail: The more sophisticated drones become, the more attractive they are to armed groups; what benefits society in progress, efficiency and safety heightens civilian risk where criminal or insurgent actors operate, producing a persistent tension between promoting advancement and mitigating weaponization.

items.label: Multilateral regulatory architecture
items.detail: The U.S.-EU Trade and Technology Council, NATO, the G7, the G20 and the WTO offer platforms to advance a shared regulatory architecture for commercial unmanned aerial systems.

items.label: NATO DIANA
items.detail: NATO's Defense Innovation Accelerator for the North Atlantic can connect governments, industry and research institutions to promote innovation while embedding safeguards against misuse.

items.label: Extend controls to subsystems and components
items.detail: Building on the 2016 Joint Declaration and taking cues from the MTCR, states should expand restrictions to cover essential subsystems and components, with regular updates reflecting technological evolution, alongside arms-control-inspired approaches emphasizing transparency, accountability and restraint.

items.label: China is the central enabler of dual-use proliferation
items.detail: It combines combat-drone exports with near-dominance of the commercial market through DJI, whose platforms are ubiquitous and routinely repurposed by both states and violent nonstate actors.

items.label: Wing Loong exports
items.detail: China has exported Wing Loong Class I combat systems to at least 17 countries.

items.label: Beijing's 2023 export controls
items.detail: From 2023 China introduced export controls on commercial drones, engines, communication gear and anti-drone systems, citing national security and its role as a responsible major country; in practice they mainly limited access in the United States as reciprocity for U.S. restrictions and in Europe, where Chinese components have been used extensively in the Russia-Ukraine war.

items.label: China-Russia drone supply relationship
items.detail: China supplies around 80 percent of critical electronics used in Russian drones, and a joint drone factory has been established in the PRC under the 'no-limits' partnership.

items.label: Market dominance
items.detail: DJI dominates more than 70 percent of the world drone market; 2022 drone sales exceeded 30.6 billion USD and its agricultural line alone had more than 200,000 units in active operation worldwide.

items.label: Israeli MALE and loitering munition exports
items.detail: Israel, among the world's top drone exporters, has supplied Heron and Hermes MALE platforms and Harop loitering munitions to numerous countries.

items.label: Hizballah
items.detail: Launched small Iranian-made UAS into Israeli airspace as early as 2006, conducted long-range surveillance flights by 2012, and in September 2014 carried out the first verified lethal drone attack by a non-state actor.

items.label: ISIS (Syria)
items.detail: Deployed DJI drones for surveillance and propaganda as early as 2014 and was successfully fielding armed drones in combat by 2017; Contested Skies II traces Colombian tactics back to methods first developed in Syria.

items.label: Turkey's loose interpretation
items.detail: Though an MTCR member, Turkey has interpreted restrictions loosely and exported Bayraktar systems across the Middle East, Africa and Eastern Europe.

items.label: Ukraine as an FPV tactics dissemination platform
items.detail: Ukraine scaled commercial platforms and FPVs into mass battlefield use and 'has become a platform for the global dissemination of FPV tactics'; a Ukrainian security official described operators learning to kill with a $400 drone and selling that knowledge to the highest bidder.

items.label: Spanish-speaking volunteers in the International Legion
items.detail: Ukrainian domestic intelligence suspects Spanish-speaking volunteers infiltrated the International Legion to train in flying FPV drones, some reportedly tied to cartels and other VNSAs.

items.label: Mavic in Ukraine and Russia
items.detail: Both Ukrainian and Russian forces deploy the Mavic extensively for battlefield reconnaissance, artillery adjustment and real-time observation, gaining tactical advantage without relying solely on expensive military-grade UAVs.

items.label: Uncertain FPV attribution
items.detail: Direct attribution of kamikaze attacks to DJI FPV models remains uncertain; open-source video from Ukraine shows them flown mostly without explosives in reconnaissance or training roles, and their small size and limited payload constrain destructive potential relative to purpose-built loitering systems, so they have served more as a technical and tactical reference inspiring improvised designs.

items.label: U.S. reclassification of the MQ-9 Reaper
items.detail: The Trump administration reclassified large, sophisticated platforms such as the MQ-9 Reaper as 'aircraft' rather than 'missile systems' to ease export restrictions and enhance competitiveness against less selective proliferators.

outline.heading: UAVs as aircraft: the common regulatory anchor

items.label: Unmanned aircraft and sUAS defined as aircraft
items.detail: Title 14 CFR defines unmanned aircraft as aircraft operated without the possibility of direct human intervention from within or on the aircraft, and sUAS as an unmanned aircraft weighing less than 55 lbs at takeoff including attached components. FAA holds authority over air traffic and general operating rules with the goal of full integration into the National Airspace System.

items.label: Weight and kinetic-energy thresholds
items.detail: The CFR uses a primary weight threshold (sUAS under 55 lbs, roughly 25 kg) plus a very small carve-out at or below 0.55 lbs; Categories 2 and 3 apply to heavier sUAS and impose restrictions based on maximum kinetic-energy transfer on impact.

outline.heading: Operational limitations: altitude, visibility and night flight

items.label: VLOS as the common baseline
items.detail: Visual line of sight is the default across all surveyed regulations; in the United States any deviation from VLOS requires a waiver.

items.label: Night operations require dedicated training
items.detail: U.S. regulations require the remote pilot to acquire specific training before conducting night operations.

items.label: Remote ID and LAANC operational nationwide
items.detail: The FAA sets the rules while industry partners provide digital services and NASA supports research; Remote ID broadcasts identification, location and control station information as a digital licence plate, and LAANC gives near real-time airspace authorisations to Part 107 pilots up to 400 ft, though BVLOS, dynamic rerouting and high-density traffic management remain in pilot phases.

items.label: Remote Pilot Certificate with Small UAS Rating
items.detail: The U.S. requires the remote pilot in command to be at least 16, to read, speak, write and understand English, to meet medical fitness requirements, and to pass an aeronautical knowledge test under 107.73 covering regulations, weather, emergency procedures, radio communications, physiological effects of drugs and alcohol, airport operations and maintenance, with recurrent training or testing every 24 calendar months. The U.S. regulatory framework does not mandate insurance for small unmanned aircraft system operations.

items.label: Explicit statutory mitigation authority
items.detail: U.S. policy guidance defines and authorises counter-UAS mitigation as the use of systems that disrupt, damage, destroy or take control of a UAS posing a threat, under authorities conferred on the Departments of Defense, Energy, Justice and Homeland Security.

items.label: DHS research and integration authority
items.detail: In 2025 the Department of Homeland Security was authorised to conduct research, development, testing and evaluation of counter-UAS technologies and to integrate operational and training activities into its nationwide mission portfolio.

items.label: Joint C-sUAS Office
items.detail: The Department of Defense established a Joint C-sUAS Office in 2019 to develop doctrine, define operational requirements, coordinate training and shape acquisition strategy.
